Digital Nomad
DIJ-ih-tul NOH-mad
noun (Millennial slang)
A remote worker who uses the internet to work from anywhere while travelling. The term was popularized by the 1997 book Digital Nomad by Tsugio Makimoto and David Manners, which predicted that technology would free workers from fixed locations. In the 2010s it became a Millennial lifestyle and industry: laptops on beaches in Bali, co-working spaces in Chiang Mai and Lisbon, travel blogs, and visas designed for remote workers. The 2020 shift to remote work multiplied its numbers.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A digital nomad works from a laptop while moving from city to city or country to country: answering email in Bali, coding in Lisbon, posting sunsets from Mexico. It is the Millennial dream of freedom from the office and the suburb. The Christian observation: remote work itself is neutral, and travel can be a gift. Paul worked as a tentmaker while moving between cities, and his travels served the gospel. But the nomadic life raises questions Scripture cares about. The first is rootedness. Even the patriarchs, who lived in tents, travelled as households with altars, and when God sent His people into a foreign land He told them to put down roots: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens … And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away" (Jer 29:5, 7). The second is community. A Christian cannot follow Christ alone. "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25) assumes a church one actually belongs to, with elders who know your name and brothers who know your sins. A digital nomad passing through a dozen cities a year can easily belong to none. The third is marriage and children, which need a place. A father can admire the adventure and still tell his son: freedom is not the absence of attachments; it is the right ones. Work hard wherever you are, but be someone’s neighbour, some church’s member, and, God willing, some child’s father in a home they can call their own.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial lifestyle term (1997 book; 2010s boom; 2020 surge) for remote workers who travel continually; remote work is neutral, but Scripture calls believers to rooted community, church membership, and seeking the peace of a place (Jer 29:5-7; Heb 10:25).

DIGITAL NOMAD, n. (term popularized 1997; Millennial lifestyle, 2010s–present) A person who works remotely via the internet while travelling from place to place. Related: remote work, co-working, wanderlust.

Webster (1828), root nomad: NOMAD, noun [Gr. Living on pasturage, to distribute or divide, to feed. This verb is connected with Latin Nemus, a wood, a place over-grown with trees, and also a pasture, the primary sense of which is probably to spring or shoot, for the verb signifies among other things, to leap, to dance, and may be allied to Eng. nimble. Cattle originally subsisted by browsing, as they still do in new settlements.] One who leads a wandering life, and subsists by tending herds of cattle which graze on herbage of spontaneous growth. […]

Decode for parents: affirm the skills; ask where your child belongs to a church and who knows him by name.

Jer 29:5 — "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them;"

Jer 29:7 — "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."

Modern Corruption

Digital nomadism prizes freedom from place and attachment; Scripture honours work and travel but calls believers to roots, a church that knows them, and households that need a home.

expand to see more

The corruption is freedom defined as unattachment. The digital nomad ideal sells a life with no fixed obligations: no office, no lease, no local community, no one depending on you. It is attractive to the young and often lonely in practice. It can postpone marriage and children indefinitely, and it makes church membership nearly impossible. A life without roots is a life without the soil in which much Christian virtue grows.

The recovery is mission and membership. Paul travelled for the gospel and stayed for years in places like Corinth and Ephesus, building churches; he was never a tourist. "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers" (Act 18:3). Christians may work remotely and travel, and they should do it as people who belong somewhere: to a local church, to a family, to a place whose peace they seek. Teach the young that roots are not a cage but a gift.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nomas (roaming in search of pasture) → nomad + Latin digitus (finger) → digital → 1997 book Digital Nomad → 2010s Millennial lifestyle → 2020 remote-work surge.
